query: For steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to corrosion? Specify a controlled study capable of revealing the governing cause, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting evidence from prior findings, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The corrosion resistance in steels for chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications is primarily due to the rapid formation and self-healing behavior of a dense, chromium-enriched oxide (mainly Cr2O3) layer that acts as a physical barrier to the ingress of corrosive species.
generation.material_initial_state: Standard corrosion‐resistant steel alloy with a nominal composition including sufficient chromium (e.g., >10 wt% Cr) and minor additions of Ni and Mo; normally endowed with its native passivation oxide layer.
generation.intervention: A controlled study in which the native oxide layer is mechanically removed (e.g., by polishing) from a set of samples; subsequently, these samples are exposed to aggressive, simulated chemical-processing or nuclear coolant environments to allow re-formation of the oxide layer. In a parallel set, additional inhibitors are added to block oxide reformation.
generation.conditions: Expose both the oxide-stripped and the control (intact oxide) specimens, as well as the inhibitor-treated group, to high-temperature (80–150 °C) corrosive media (acidic or simulated nuclear coolant solutions) under static or controlled flow conditions for a period (e.g., 100 hours) that is sufficient to monitor initial passivation and subsequent corrosion rates.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation and integrity of the Cr2O3-based passivating oxide film at the steel surface.
generation.mechanism: Oxygen and other oxidizing species rapidly react with the surface chromium to form a dense and self-healing Cr2O3 layer. This layer limits the diffusion of corrosive species (such as oxygen and chloride ions), thereby impeding the electrochemical reactions that lead to corrosion of the underlying steel.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples with their native or rapidly reformed oxide layer will exhibit significantly lower corrosion rates compared to those where the passivating film has been removed or its reformation chemically inhibited. In addition, spectroscopy and impedance measurements should show quicker re-establishment and greater stability of the Cr2O3 film on untreated samples relative to inhibited samples.
generation.baseline: Steel with its original, intact passivation oxide layer under the same environmental conditions.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis holds for steels with sufficient chromium content and under environmental conditions typical of chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications. Its applicability may be limited outside the specified temperature range, in environments with drastically different corrosive aggressiveness, or in steels with substantially different alloying compositions that do not favor Cr2O3 formation.
generation.uncertainty: While the formation of the Cr2O3 layer is well-known, the precise kinetics of self-healing under varying dynamic stresses and in the presence of minor alloying elements remains uncertain. Furthermore, the interplay between mechanical stripping of the oxide and its subsequent reformation under operational stresses could introduce variability.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare three groups of steel samples: (1) untreated (with native oxide layer intact), (2) oxide-stripped by mechanical polishing, and (3) oxide-stripped with the addition of a surface inhibitor designed to block oxide reformation. Expose all groups to a simulated corrosive environment (acidic or nuclear coolant mimic) at 80–150 °C for 100 hours. Monitor the surface oxidation using XPS and measure corrosion rates via weight loss and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy.
measurements: Weight loss over time to quantify corrosion rates
XPS analysis to monitor the reformation and composition of the oxide film
Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy to assess the integrity and barrier properties of the surface film
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples without the passivating oxide (or with blocked reformation) do not show statistically higher corrosion rates or if XPS and impedance measurements indicate similar oxide formation and barrier properties as the untreated control, then the hypothesis that the Cr2O3 passivation layer is the primary mechanism for corrosion resistance would be falsified.
